title: My Horse Was Death’s Broker
intro: These six verses circulate in Antarah's name in a poem beginning “When time lifts its veil for you”. Yaqut quotes three of them under al-Masani' in his geographical dictionary. All six close a fourteen-verse poem in the Beirut diwan, a collection that draws on the hero's popular romance as well as his transmitted poetry. Their attribution remains provisional. The boast moves from a horse trading on a battlefield to a whole country shrinking around a fleeing opponent.

translation: He plunged into its dust, buying and selling.
1.sharh: In the preceding verse of the printed poem the spears set up a market and lives are its merchandise. The horse rides into its dust and does business on both sides of the bargain.

translation: My sword was a physician in the mêlée,
treating the head of anyone who complained of a headache.
2.sharh: The verse sounds almost solicitous, down to naming the patient's complaint. The listener has to supply the dreadful sense in which a sword can put an end to a headache.

translation: I am the slave you have heard about.
Now you have seen me. Set hearsay aside.
3.sharh: The speaker takes up the very name an opponent might use to belittle him. Seeing what the man can do will settle what talk of “the slave” is worth.

translation: If I sent my spear out with a coward,
he would face wild beasts on the strength of my name.
4.sharh: Even with a different man carrying the spear, the fear its owner inspires would travel with it. The boast depends on the new bearer being a coward.

translation: I filled the earth with dread of my blade.
My opponent found no room in it.
5.sharh: What fills the earth is fear. Seen from the enemy's side, that same expanse offers nowhere to go, a thought the next verse turns into a physical measurement.

translation: When champions flee for fear of my might,
they see whole lands as a fathom or a cubit.
6.sharh: The dimensions keep shrinking. First a whole region seems only the span of two outstretched arms, then only the length from elbow to fingertip.

1.1.3.head: دَلّال
1.1.3.meaning: A broker who brings buyer and seller together and calls out the wares.

1.1.4.meaning: Deaths, pictured here as the fates awaiting individual riders.

1.2.3.head: شَرى
1.2.3.meaning: Bought. The word can also mean “sold”, but the next verb supplies that side of the transaction.

2.1.4.meaning: Battle at its height. Yaqut's quotation places the sword “in the open desert”.

2.2.5.head: الصُّداع
2.2.5.meaning: A headache, the complaint on which the grim joke about a doctor turns.

3.1.4.head: خُبِّرَ
3.1.4.meaning: Were told, as one hears news of somebody absent.

3.2.2.head: عايَنَ
3.2.2.meaning: Saw with your own eyes, with the force of an eyewitness confronting hearsay.

4.1.3.head: رُمح
4.1.3.meaning: A spear. In the passage quoted by Yaqut the coward carries a sword.

4.1.4.head: مَعَ
4.1.4.meaning: With. The singer pronounces this as one closed syllable before “a coward”. Classical grammarians also record this pronunciation.

5.2.5.head: اِتِّساع
5.2.5.meaning: Room to move or get away.

6.2.2.head: الأَقطار
6.2.2.meaning: Far reaches or regions of the earth.

6.2.3.head: باع
6.2.3.meaning: A fathom, the span from fingertip to fingertip with both arms outstretched.

6.2.5.head: ذِراع
6.2.5.meaning: A cubit, measured from elbow to the tip of the middle finger.
